sentences.t: When I was twenty-five I thought I was really good with money, and then I did my own taxes and found out I was not.
So here are seven mistakes I made, what they cost me, and what I'd do differently.
Mistake number one, I didn't adjust my withholding when I started freelancing on the side.
Nobody was taking taxes out of that side money, so in April I owed almost four thousand dollars I did not have.
If you have any income that isn't on a regular paycheck, set aside like twenty-five percent of it the day it lands.
Mistake number two, I didn't make quarterly estimated payments, so on top of owing the money, I got hit with an underpayment penalty.
It wasn't huge, but it's literally paying extra for being disorganized.
Mistake number three, and this one hurts, I wasn't putting anything into my employer's retirement plan even though they matched up to four percent.
That's free money, and I left it on the table for two whole years.
Okay, mistake number four, and this is the one that actually scared me.
Right around tax season I got an email that looked exactly like it came from the IRS, saying my refund was on hold and I needed to verify my identity.
And I was stressed, I was behind, so I clicked it and typed in my Social Security number.
Two weeks later someone had filed a return in my name and collected a refund that was supposed to be mine.
Fixing that took eight months, a stack of forms, and a lot of hold music.
And that whole mess is honestly the reason I take protecting my identity way more seriously now.

Alright, mistake number five.
I didn't keep any receipts for my freelance expenses, so I couldn't deduct things I absolutely could have.
Software, a chunk of my phone bill, the laptop I bought for the work, all of it gone because I had nothing to prove it.
Now I just take a photo of every receipt and drop it in one folder, it takes five seconds.
Mistake number six, I let a lifestyle upgrade eat my entire raise.
I got a ten percent bump and immediately leased a nicer car, so I had more income and somehow less money.
And mistake number seven, I didn't open a Roth IRA when my income was low enough to qualify easily.
Those early years are when your money has the most time to grow, and I spent them on concert tickets.
Which, to be fair, some of those concerts were great.
If you're in your twenties and you only fix one thing on this list, fix the retirement match, it's the easiest win there is.
